newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb hardliners expel Plavsic in power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Serb hardliners expel Plavsic in power struggle.

text.p: Bosnian Serb hardliners, waging a battle for power, have expelled President Biljana Plavsic from their ruling party and demanded she step down from office, a party official said on Sunday.

"The executive committee at yesterday's session unanimously decided to expel Biljana Plavsic from the SDS and we repeated our appeal to transfer her authorities to Vice-President Dragoljub Mirjanic," Vlado Verkes, secretary-general of the party, told reporters.
The ultra-nationalist Serb Democratic Party (SDS), which rules Bosnia's Serb entity, is run by hardliners loyal to former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
The vote to kick Plavsic out of the party followed outspoken attacks on Karadzic at rallies and her comments in an interview threatening to arrest Karadzic and his allies for rampant corruption.

Although long expected, the decision underlined frustration among Karadzic loyalists who have failed to broker a compromise solution to the conflict with Plavsic. Hardliners had already excluded her from decision making in the SDS.

Plavsic has also angered Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic by publicly identifying him as the guiding force behind Serb nationalism in Bosnia despite his denials of responsibility for the 1992-95 war.

Her accusations of corruption have tapped strong public support among ordinary Bosnian Serbs, many of them living at subsistence levels in contrast with the wealth flaunted by Karadzic and his allies.

Opposition parties and some regional SDS officials, especially in the northwest region around Banja Luka, have thrown their support behind Plavsic since she tried to suspend the interior minister, Dragan Kijac, a Karadzic loyalist.

The move against Plavsic risked splitting the Bosnian Serb entity in two, with rival governments in Banja Luka where she is based and Pale, the hardliners' stronghold outside Sarajeveo to the southeast.
The expulsion does not effect her legal position as president. The constitution requires the parliament to call a referendum to remove the president.
Plavsic dissolved the parliament and called for elections on September 1. Western peace mediators said her move was legal but the hardliners refused to recognise her decision.
The constitutional court froze her decision pending a final ruling.
Hardliners have accused Plavsic of being too cooperative with international mediators who also want to arrest Karadzic and other indicted Serbs for trial by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
Their fears have hardened since British troops captured a war crimes suspect in the northern town of Prijedor this month and shot dead another who resisted arrest.
NATO soldiers and international observers have been the target of a series of minor retaliatory explosions over the past week.
Two explosions were heard in Banja Luka overnight but NATO said no international agency was targeted and no injuries were reported.
United States diplomats issued a stern warning to the Serb leadership in talks on Saturday, demanding a halt to the retaliation campaign, Western officials said.
An American soldier was slightly injured in an explosion on Friday evening and another suffered a minor wound when he was struck from behind with a sickle on Serb territory.
